subject: chemistry
title: Solid State
boardNote: Covers all four recent papers: 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

examMarks.basis: Chapter 1 questions in the 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers: 7, 5, 5 and 5 marks

stops.title: Crystalline & amorphous solids; isomorphism & polymorphism
stops.inShort: Crystalline solids have long-range order, sharp melting points and anisotropy (except cubic); amorphous solids are supercooled liquids with short-range order, a melting range and isotropy. Isomorphous pairs share a crystal structure; polymorphs are different crystalline forms of the same substance.

cards.text: Constituent particles (atoms, ions or molecules) have a regular, periodic long-range arrangement. Crystalline solids melt sharply at a definite temperature and, except for cubic crystals, are anisotropic—properties like refractive index and conductivity vary with direction. Examples: NaCl, ice, metals (Na, Cu, Au), diamond and graphite.

Particles are randomly arranged with only short-range order, making amorphous solids supercooled liquids. They soften and melt gradually over a temperature range and are isotropic (same magnitude of physical properties in every direction). Examples: glass, plastic, rubber, tar and metallic glass.

Two or more substances having the same crystal structure and the same atomic ratio are isomorphous (e.g. NaF & MgO in 1:1 ratio; NaNO_{3} & CaCO_{3} in 1:1:3 ratio). A single substance existing in two or more crystalline forms is polymorphous (calcite & aragonite for CaCO_{3}; α-quartz, β-quartz & cristobalite for SiO_{2}). Polymorphism in elements is allotropy (diamond, graphite, fullerene).

checks.q: Which pair of substances is isomorphous with the same 1 : 1 : 3 atomic ratio?
checks.hint: Isomorphous substances are two different compounds with the same crystal structure and same atomic ratio.
checks.explain: NaNO_{3} and CaCO_{3} are different substances sharing the same crystal structure and the same 1 : 1 : 3 atomic ratio. Calcite/aragonite and diamond/graphite are polymorphs of a single substance.

checks.q: All crystalline solids, including those with a cubic crystal structure, are anisotropic.
checks.hint: Check the exception stated in Balbharati Section 1.2.1.
checks.explain: False. All crystalline substances except those having a cubic structure are anisotropic; cubic crystals are isotropic because of their high symmetry.

checks.q: Why are amorphous solids such as glass called isotropic?
options: They melt at a single sharp temperature
Their physical properties have the same magnitude in all directions
Their constituent particles have long-range periodic order
They always consist of a single large crystal
checks.hint: Recall the meaning of 'iso-' (same) and 'tropic' (direction).
checks.explain: Because particles in an amorphous solid are randomly arranged with no long-range order, properties such as refractive index and conductivity are independent of the direction of measurement.

stops.title: Classification of crystalline solids
stops.inShort: Crystalline solids are classified into four types by their particles and bonding: ionic (cations/anions, electrostatic), covalent network (atoms, 3D covalent bonds), molecular (molecules, weak intermolecular forces) and metallic (metal cations in a sea of mobile electrons).

cards.text: Ionic crystals (NaCl, KCl, CaF_{2}, K_{2}SO_{4}) consist of cations and anions held by strong electrostatic forces; they are hard, brittle, high-melting, and conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved in water. Covalent network solids (diamond, quartz SiO_{2}, BN, carborundum) are giant 3D covalently bonded molecules—the hardest, high-melting, and poor conductors (exceptions: graphite conducts electricity; diamond conducts heat well).

Constituent particles are molecules (or monoatomic noble gas atoms such as Ar, Ne) held together by weak intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces in nonpolar solids (CH_{4}, H_{2}, CO_{2}), dipole-dipole forces in polar solids (HCl, SO_{2}), or intermolecular hydrogen bonds (H_{2}O ice, NH_{3}, HF). They are soft, low-melting and poor electrical conductors.

Formed by atoms of a metallic element whose valence electrons are delocalised over the whole crystal, leaving positive metal ions immersed in a sea of mobile electrons. Metallic crystals (Na, Mg, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au) are malleable, ductile, and good conductors of heat and electricity, with wide ranges of hardness and melting point.

checks.q: A solid is hard, brittle and an electrical insulator in the solid state, but its melt conducts electricity well. What type of crystalline solid is it?
checks.hint: Which solids have immobile ions in the solid state that become free to move on melting?
checks.explain: Ionic solids have cations and anions locked in a rigid lattice (hard, brittle, non-conducting solid), but on melting or dissolving in water the ions become mobile and conduct electricity.

checks.q: Which intermolecular force holds the molecules together in solid H_{2}O (ice), solid NH_{3} and solid HF?
checks.hint: H is covalently bonded to strongly electronegative O, N or F.
checks.explain: Solid H_{2}O (ice), NH_{3} and HF are hydrogen-bonded molecular crystals held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

checks.q: Just like ionic solids, covalent network solids show an abrupt rise in electrical conductivity as soon as they are melted.
checks.hint: Check how electrical properties distinguish ionic crystals from covalent network crystals on page 4.
checks.explain: False. Ionic solids become good conductors abruptly above their melting points, whereas covalent network solids show low conductivity that rises gradually with temperature with no abrupt jump on melting.

stops.title: Crystal lattice, basis, unit cells & 7 crystal systems
stops.inShort: Crystal = Lattice + Basis. The unit cell is the smallest repeating 3D structural unit, specified by edge lengths a, b, c and angles α, β, γ. Four unit-cell types (primitive, body-centred, face-centred, base-centred) give 14 Bravais lattices across 7 crystal systems.

cards.text: A space lattice is a three-dimensional periodic geometrical array of points. The constituent particles attached to every lattice point form the basis. Combining the two generates the crystal: Lattice + Basis = Crystal.

cards.t: Unit cell and its four types
cards.text: The smallest repeating structural unit of a crystalline solid is the unit cell, specified by axial lengths a, b, c and interaxial angles α, β, γ (Fig 1.1). Its four types are: primitive (corners only), body-centred (corners + 1 body centre), face-centred (corners + 6 face centres) and base-centred (corners + 2 opposite face centres).

cards.t: Seven crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices
cards.text: Only 14 distinct three-dimensional space lattices (Bravais lattices) exist. They are grouped into 7 crystal systems: cubic (3), orthorhombic (4), tetragonal (2), monoclinic (2), rhombohedral (1), triclinic (1) and hexagonal (1).

checks.q: Which of the seven crystal systems possesses all four Bravais lattice types (primitive, body-centred, face-centred and base-centred)?
checks.hint: Count the Bravais lattices for each crystal system in the chart on page 7.
checks.explain: Orthorhombic has all 4 Bravais lattices. Cubic has 3 (sc, bcc, fcc), tetragonal has 2 (simple, body-centred), and monoclinic has 2 (simple, base-centred).

checks.q: How many distinct three-dimensional Bravais lattices are possible across all seven crystal systems?
checks.hint: Add the Bravais lattices of cubic (3), orthorhombic (4), tetragonal (2), monoclinic (2), rhombohedral (1), triclinic (1) and hexagonal (1).
checks.explain: By mathematical analysis, there are exactly 14 Bravais lattices distributed across the 7 crystal systems.

checks.q: A base-centred unit cell has constituent particles at its eight corners and at the centres of all six faces.
checks.hint: Compare the definitions of face-centred and base-centred unit cells on page 6.
checks.explain: False. A base-centred unit cell has particles at the centres of any two opposite faces (in addition to the corners). Particles at all six face centres define a face-centred unit cell.

stops.title: Number of particles in SC, BCC & FCC cubic unit cells
sections: 1.5.1 Number of Particles in Cubic Unit Cells
stops.inShort: In a cubic lattice, each corner contributes 1/8, each face-centre 1/2, each edge-centre 1/4, and the body-centre 1. Thus simple cubic (sc) has n = 1, body-centred cubic (bcc) has n = 2, and face-centred cubic (fcc) has n = 4 particles per unit cell.

cards.t: Sharing of lattice positions in a cube
cards.text: When cubic unit cells are stacked in 3D, each corner particle is shared by 8 cubes (contributes 1/8), each face-centre particle by 2 cubes (contributes 1/2), each edge-centre particle by 4 cubes (contributes 1/4), and a body-centre particle belongs solely to 1 cube (contributes 1).

cards.t: Particles in sc and bcc unit cells
cards.text: A simple cubic (sc) unit cell has 8 corner particles, giving n = (1/8) × 8 = 1 particle per unit cell. A body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell has 8 corners plus 1 unshared body-centre particle, giving n = (1/8) × 8 + 1 = 2 particles per unit cell.

cards.t: Particles in fcc unit cell and compound formulas
cards.text: A face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cell has 8 corners plus 6 face-centre particles, giving n = (1/8) × 8 + (1/2) × 6 = 1 + 3 = 4 particles per unit cell. Counting each element's contributions gives the compound formula (e.g. C at 8 corners = 1 and D at 6 faces = 3 gives CD_{3}).

checks.q: Find the total number of particles n belonging to one body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell.
checks.hint: Add the contribution of 8 corners (1/8 each) and 1 body-centre particle (1).
checks.explain: n = 8 × (1/8) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 particles per bcc unit cell.

checks.q: A crystalline compound of elements C and D has C atoms at all 8 corners and D atoms at the centres of all 6 faces of a cubic unit cell. What is the formula of the compound?
checks.hint: Multiply corners by 1/8 and face centres by 1/2.
checks.explain: C atoms per unit cell = 8 × (1/8) = 1. D atoms per unit cell = 6 × (1/2) = 3. Hence the formula is CD_{3} (Problem 1.2).

checks.q: Which calculation correctly gives the number of particles per face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cell?
checks.hint: Each of 8 corners contributes 1/8 and each of 6 faces contributes 1/2.
checks.explain: Corner particles contribute 8 × (1/8) = 1 and six face-centre particles contribute 6 × (1/2) = 3, giving 1 + 3 = 4 particles per fcc unit cell.

stops.title: Density, molar mass & edge length relation
sections: 1.5.2 Relationship Between Molar Mass, Density of the Substance and Unit Cell Edge Length
stops.inShort: Mass of one particle is m = M/N_{A}, mass of a cubic unit cell is nm, and its volume is a³. Hence density ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}), linking molar mass M, density ρ, edge length a and lattice type n.

cards.t: Mass and volume of a cubic unit cell
cards.text: For a cubic unit cell of edge length a, the volume is a³. If one particle has mass m and the unit cell contains n particles, then mass of unit cell = m × n, and the crystal density is ρ = (m × n) / a³.

One mole contains N_{A} = 6.022 × 10^{23} particles, so molar mass M = m × N_{A}, giving m = M / N_{A}. Substituting into the density expression gives ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}). Knowing any four quantities determines the fifth.

cards.t: Unit conversions and identifying the lattice
cards.text: Always convert edge length from picometres to centimetres using 1 pm = 10^{-12} m = 10^{-10} cm so that M in g mol^{-1} yields ρ in g cm^{-3} (1 g cm^{-3} = 10^{3} kg m^{-3}). Solving n = ρ a³ N_{A} / M identifies the cubic lattice: n = 1 (sc), n = 2 (bcc), n = 4 (fcc).

checks.q: A metal of molar mass 50 g mol^{-1} crystallises in a bcc lattice (n = 2) with unit cell edge length 300 pm. Calculate its density ρ (use N_{A} = 6.022 × 10^{23} mol^{-1}).
checks.hint: Convert a = 300 pm = 3.00 × 10^{-8} cm, then use ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}).

checks.q: Given density ρ, edge length a, molar mass M and Avogadro number N_{A}, which formula solves for the number of particles n per unit cell?
checks.hint: Rearrange ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) to isolate n.
checks.explain: Multiplying both sides of ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) by a³ N_{A} and dividing by M gives n = ρ a³ N_{A} / M.

checks.q: To calculate density in g cm^{-3} using ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) with M in g mol^{-1}, an edge length of 400 pm must be substituted as:

stops.title: Close packing in 1D, 2D & 3D; coordination number & voids
sections: 1.6 Packing of Particles in Crystal Lattice
1.6.2 Coordination Number in Close Packed Structure
1.6.3 Number of Voids per Atom in hcp and ccp
stops.inShort: 2D square packing (CN 4) stacks AAAA to form simple cubic (CN 6, Po). 2D hexagonal packing (CN 6) stacks ABAB for hcp (Mg, Zn) or ABCABC for ccp/fcc (Cu, Ag), both with CN 12. For N atoms in hcp/ccp, there are 2N tetrahedral voids and N octahedral voids.

cards.text: In 1D, spheres touch in a straight row (Fig 1.3(a)). In 2D, aligning rows directly (AAAA...) gives square close packing with CN = 4 (Fig 1.3(b)); fitting the second row into depressions of the first (ABAB...) gives hexagonal close packing with CN = 6 (Fig 1.3(c)), leaving smaller triangular voids and tighter packing.

Stacking 2D square layers directly (AAAA...) gives simple cubic (CN = 6; polonium is the only metal with sc). Stacking 2D hexagonal layers with the third layer aligned over the first gives ABAB... hcp (Mg, Zn); placing the third layer over octahedral voids gives ABCABC... ccp/fcc (Cu, Ag). Both hcp and ccp/fcc have CN = 12 (6 in own layer, 3 above, 3 below).

When layer B rests in depressions of layer A, covered triangular voids become tetrahedral voids (surrounded by 4 spheres, Fig 1.6) while uncovered overlapping triangular voids of both layers form octahedral voids (surrounded by 6 spheres, Fig 1.7). For N close-packed particles in hcp or ccp, there are 2N tetrahedral voids and N octahedral voids.

checks.q: What are the layer stacking pattern and coordination number in a cubic close-packed (ccp/fcc) metal such as Cu or Ag?
checks.hint: In ccp, the third layer covers the octahedral voids of the first two layers, so the fourth layer aligns with the first.
checks.explain: Covering octahedral voids gives the ABCABC... stacking pattern of ccp/fcc, where each sphere touches 12 neighbours (6 in its own layer, 3 above, 3 below).

checks.q: A compound is formed by elements A and B. Atoms of B form a ccp structure and atoms of A occupy one-third (1/3) of the tetrahedral voids. What is the formula of the compound?
checks.hint: Each B atom generates 2 tetrahedral voids, so A = (1/3) × 2B.
checks.explain: Number of tetrahedral voids = 2B. Atoms of A occupy 1/3 of them, so A = (2/3)B. Thus A : B = 2/3 : 1 = 2 : 3, giving formula A_{2}B_{3} (Problem 1.4).

checks.q: An octahedral void is surrounded by six close-packed spheres, and for N atoms in an hcp or ccp structure there are N octahedral voids.
checks.hint: Compare tetrahedral voids (4 spheres, 2N) with octahedral voids (6 spheres, N).
checks.explain: True. Overlapping triangular voids from two adjacent hexagonal layers are enclosed by 6 spheres, producing 1 octahedral void per atom (N voids for N atoms).

stops.title: Packing efficiency of SC, BCC & FCC lattices
sections: 1.7.1 Packing Efficiency of Metal Crystal in Simple Cubic Lattice
1.7.2 Packing Efficiency of Metal Crystal in Body-Centred Cubic Lattice
1.7.3 Packing Efficiency of Metal Crystal in Face-Centred Cubic Lattice
stops.inShort: Packing efficiency = (volume of particles in unit cell / a³) × 100. sc: r = a/2, 52.36% occupied (47.64% void). bcc: r = (√3/4)a, 68% occupied (32% void). fcc/ccp/hcp: r = a/(2√2), 74% occupied (26% void).

cards.text: Corner spheres touch along the edge (Fig 1.9), so a = 2r, i.e. r = a/2 = 0.5000a. With n = 1, volume occupied is (4/3)π(a/2)³ = πa³/6. Packing efficiency = (π/6) × 100 = 52.36%, leaving 47.64% void volume.

The body-centre sphere touches two corner spheres along the cube body diagonal of length √3 a (Fig 1.10), so 4r = √3 a and r = (√3/4)a = 0.4330a. With n = 2, occupied volume is (√3 π a³)/8, giving packing efficiency = (√3 π/8) × 100 = 68% and void volume = 32%.

Corner spheres touch the face-centre sphere along the face diagonal of length √2 a (Fig 1.11), so 4r = √2 a and r = a/(2√2) = 0.3535a. With n = 4, occupied volume is πa³/(3√2), giving packing efficiency = [π/(3√2)] × 100 = 74% (most efficient) and void volume = 26%.

checks.q: Lead (Pb) has an fcc structure with unit cell edge length a = 495 pm. Calculate the radius r of a Pb atom (to the nearest whole number).
In a crystal lattice formed by body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cells, what is the percentage of empty space (void volume)?
checks.hint: Subtract the bcc packing efficiency (68%) from 100%.
checks.explain: In a bcc unit cell, 68% of total space is occupied by particles and 100 − 68 = 32% is empty void volume.

checks.q: Among sc, bcc and fcc crystal lattices, fcc/ccp/hcp makes the most efficient use of space (74%) while simple cubic makes the least efficient use (52.36%).
checks.hint: Compare 52.36% (sc), 68% (bcc) and 74% (fcc/ccp/hcp).
checks.explain: True. Packing efficiency rises from 52.36% in sc to 68% in bcc and reaches the maximum 74% in fcc/ccp/hcp.

stops.title: Number of particles & unit cells in x g of metal
sections: 1.7.4 Number of Particles and Unit Cells in x g of Metallic Crystal
stops.inShort: Substituting M = ρ a³ N_{A} / n into xN_{A}/M gives: particles in x g = xn / (ρa³), unit cells in x g = x / (ρa³), and unit cells in volume V = V / a³.

cards.t: Number of particles in x g of metal
cards.text: Since molar mass M contains N_{A} particles, x g of metal contains xN_{A}/M particles. From the density formula, M = ρ a³ N_{A} / n. Substituting M cancels N_{A} and yields: Number of particles in x g = xn / (ρa³).

cards.t: Number of unit cells in x g of metal
cards.text: Because n particles make 1 unit cell, dividing the number of particles by n gives: Number of unit cells in x g = x / (ρa³). Equivalently, x/ρ is the sample volume V, divided by one unit cell's volume a³.

cards.t: Unit cells in a given volume V
cards.text: When the volume V of a metal sample is given directly (e.g. 1.00 cm³), the number of unit cells is simply V / a³. Always express a in cm when V is in cm³ and ρ is in g cm^{-3}.

checks.q: Starting from xN_{A}/M particles in x g of metal, which expression for M is substituted to obtain xn / (ρa³)?
checks.hint: Solve ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) for M.
checks.explain: From ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}), we get M = ρ a³ N_{A} / n. Substituting into xN_{A}/M cancels N_{A} and gives xn / (ρa³).

checks.q: A metal crystal has cubic unit cell volume a³ = 6.4 × 10^{-23} cm³. Calculate the number of unit cells in 1.28 cm³ of the metal, expressed as a multiple of 10^{22}.
checks.hint: Number of unit cells in volume V is V / a³.

checks.q: Which formula gives the number of unit cells present in x g of a metal having density ρ and cubic unit cell edge length a?
checks.hint: Divide the number of particles xn / (ρa³) by n particles per unit cell.
checks.explain: Since n particles correspond to 1 unit cell, dividing xn / (ρa³) by n gives x / (ρa³) unit cells.

stops.title: Point defects: Schottky, Frenkel, impurity & non-stoichiometric
stops.inShort: Point defects preserve electrical neutrality. Stoichiometric defects keep formula ratio fixed: vacancy, self-interstitial, Schottky (paired vacancies, lowers density: NaCl, KCl, AgBr) and Frenkel (cation in interstitial void, density unchanged: ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI, CaF_{2}). Impurity defects are substitutional (brass, SrCl_{2} in NaCl) or interstitial (C in steel). Non-stoichiometric defects are metal deficiency (Ni_{0.97}O_{1.0}) and metal excess (Zn_{1+x}O_{1.0}, F-centres in NaCl).

cards.text: Schottky defect is a paired cation–anion vacancy in highly ionic crystals with high CN and similar ion sizes (NaCl, KCl, AgBr); it lowers density while preserving electrical neutrality. Frenkel defect occurs when a smaller cation shifts from its lattice site to an interstitial void in low-CN crystals with large size difference (ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI, CaF_{2}); density and neutrality remain unchanged.

Substitutional impurity defects occur when foreign atoms replace host atoms at regular lattice sites—e.g. Zn replacing Cu in brass (Fig 1.17), or aliovalent Sr^{2+} replacing two Na^{+} ions in NaCl to create one cation vacancy (Fig 1.18). Interstitial impurity defects occur when foreign atoms occupy interstitial voids—e.g. C atoms in the Fe lattice of steel (Fig 1.19).

Metal deficiency defect occurs in variable-valency metals: missing Ni^{2+} in NiO is balanced by two Ni^{3+} ions, giving Ni_{0.97}O_{1.0}. Metal excess defect occurs either via interstitial metal atoms/cations + electrons (ZnO → Zn^{2+} + ½O_{2} + 2e^{-}, giving Zn_{1+x}O_{1.0}) or via anion vacancies trapping electrons called F-centres (heating NaCl in Na vapour gives yellow Na_{1+x}Cl_{1.0}).

checks.q: Which ionic solid exhibits BOTH Schottky defect and Frenkel defect?
checks.hint: Check the examples listed under both Schottky defect and Frenkel defect on page 18.
checks.explain: AgBr appears in the examples of both Schottky defect (NaCl, AgBr, KCl) and Frenkel defect (ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI, CaF_{2}).

checks.q: Frenkel defect decreases the density of an ionic crystal because cations move away from their regular lattice sites.
checks.hint: Does the displaced cation leave the crystal, or stay inside an interstitial void?
checks.explain: False. In a Frenkel defect no ion leaves the crystal lattice as a whole—the cation merely shifts to an interstitial position—so the density remains unchanged.

checks.q: When a small amount of SrCl_{2} is added to NaCl during crystallisation, how is electrical neutrality maintained?
options: Each Sr^{2+} ion replaces one Na^{+} ion
Each Sr^{2+} ion displaces two Na^{+} ions, occupying one site and leaving the second site vacant
Each Sr^{2+} ion enters an interstitial site without removing any Na^{+} ion
Two Sr^{2+} ions replace one Na^{+} ion
checks.hint: Compare the +2 charge of Sr^{2+} with the +1 charge of Na^{+}.
checks.explain: To balance +2 charge, every Sr^{2+} removes two Na^{+} ions: Sr^{2+} occupies one Na^{+} site and the other site remains a cation vacancy (Fig 1.18).

stops.title: Electrical properties & band theory
stops.inShort: Conductivities span conductors (10^{4}–10^{7}), semiconductors (10^{-6}–10^{4}) and insulators (10^{-20}–10^{-10} Ω^{-1}m^{-1}). Overlapping atomic orbitals form valence and conduction bands separated by a band gap: zero/overlapping in metals, small in semiconductors (Si, Ge), large forbidden zone in insulators. Raising temperature lowers metallic conductivity but increases semiconductor conductivity.

cards.text: Solids are classified by conductivity (Ω^{-1}m^{-1}): conductors (10^{4}–10^{7}), semiconductors (10^{-6}–10^{4}) and insulators (10^{-20}–10^{-10}). Overlapping atomic orbitals form closely spaced energy bands: a lower-energy valence band (bound electrons) and a higher-energy conduction band (mobile delocalised electrons), separated by the band gap.

Metals have a partially filled conduction band (e.g. 3s band in Na, E_{gap} = 0) or overlapping filled and empty bands (e.g. filled 3s and vacant 3p in Mg), allowing free electron flow. Insulators have a filled valence band and empty conduction band separated by a large forbidden zone (e.g. diamond 5.47 eV) that thermal energy cannot bridge.

Pure semiconductors (Si: E_{gap} = 1.12 eV; Ge: 0.67 eV) have a small band gap, so above 0 K some electrons thermally jump to the conduction band. Heating increases semiconductor conductivity (more electrons promoted), whereas heating decreases metallic conductivity (stronger lattice cation vibrations interrupt electron flow).

checks.q: How does increasing temperature affect the electrical conductivity of a metal and of an intrinsic semiconductor?
options: Decreases for a metal and increases for a semiconductor
Increases for a metal and decreases for a semiconductor
checks.hint: Think of lattice vibrations in metals versus thermal promotion across the small band gap in semiconductors.
checks.explain: Higher temperature increases metal-cation vibrations (lowering metallic conductivity) but promotes more electrons across the small band gap in a semiconductor (raising semiconductor conductivity).

checks.q: What is the electrical conductivity range (in Ω^{-1} m^{-1}) of semiconductors according to Balbharati?
checks.hint: Semiconductors lie intermediate between insulators (10^{-20}–10^{-10}) and conductors (10^{4}–10^{7}).
checks.explain: Semiconductors have conductivities in the intermediate range 10^{-6} to 10^{4} Ω^{-1} m^{-1}.

checks.q: In metallic magnesium, conduction occurs because the completely filled 3s band overlaps with the vacant 3p band.
checks.hint: Check the magnesium example in the 'Do you know?' box on page 22.
checks.explain: True. Mg ([Ar]3s²3p⁰) has a completely filled 3s band overlapping a vacant 3p band, allowing higher-energy electrons to move freely into the 3p band.

stops.title: Extrinsic semiconductors & magnetic properties
stops.inShort: Doping group-14 Si/Ge with group-15 elements (P, As, Sb, Bi) gives n-type semiconductors (extra electrons); doping with group-13 elements (B, Ga, In) gives p-type (positively behaving holes). Solids are diamagnetic (paired electrons, weakly repelled), paramagnetic (unpaired, weakly attracted) or ferromagnetic (many unpaired, strongly and permanently magnetised).

cards.text: Adding a minute amount of impurity (dopant) to an intrinsic semiconductor creates an extrinsic semiconductor with much higher conductivity. Doping group-14 Si or Ge with group-15 elements (P, As, Sb, Bi; 5 valence electrons) uses 4 electrons for bonding and places 1 extra electron in the conduction band—an n-type semiconductor (Fig 1.26, 1.27).

Doping Si or Ge with group-13 elements (B, Ga, In; 3 valence electrons) leaves one covalent bond short of an electron, creating a vacancy called a hole in the valence band (Fig 1.28). Holes accept nearby electrons and behave like mobile positive charge carriers. Both n-type and p-type semiconductors remain electrically neutral overall.

Spinning unpaired electrons act like tiny magnets. Diamagnetic solids have all electrons paired and are weakly repelled (N_{2}, F_{2}, NaCl, H_{2}O, benzene). Paramagnetic solids have unpaired electrons and are weakly attracted only in an external magnetic field (O_{2}, Cu^{2+}, Fe^{3+}, Cr^{3+}). Ferromagnetic solids have many unpaired electrons, are strongly attracted, and retain permanent magnetism (Fe, Co, Ni, Gd, CrO_{2}).

checks.q: Which of the following is an n-type semiconductor?
checks.hint: n-type needs a group-15 dopant (P, As, Sb, Bi) added to group-14 Si or Ge.
checks.explain: Arsenic (As) belongs to group 15 (5 valence electrons), so Si doped with As has extra electrons in the conduction band and is n-type. Ga and In are group-13 dopants (p-type).

checks.q: Which group contains ONLY ferromagnetic substances as listed in the textbook?
checks.hint: Ferromagnetic substances can be permanently magnetised.
checks.explain: Fe, Co, Ni, Gd and CrO_{2} are ferromagnetic. O_{2}, Cu^{2+}, Fe^{3+} and Cr^{3+} are paramagnetic; NaCl, H_{2}O, N_{2} and benzene are diamagnetic.

checks.q: An n-type semiconductor carries a net negative electrical charge, while a p-type semiconductor carries a net positive charge.
checks.hint: Both host atoms and dopant atoms are electrically neutral.
checks.explain: False. Whether intrinsic or extrinsic (n-type or p-type), the semiconductor crystal as a whole is electrically neutral; 'n' and 'p' refer only to the sign of the majority mobile charge carriers.

stops.title: Chapter exercises & mixed board problems
stops.inShort: End-of-chapter mixed MCQs, short answers and numericals combining unit-cell geometry, density, voids, defects, band theory and magnetic properties. Watch pm-to-cm conversions and particle count n.

cards.text: Keep these side by side: sc (n = 1, CN = 6, r = a/2, PE = 52.36%, void = 47.64%), bcc (n = 2, CN = 8, r = (√3/4)a, PE = 68%, void = 32%), fcc/ccp (n = 4, CN = 12, r = a/(2√2) = 0.3535a, PE = 74%, void = 26%).

Density ρ = nM/(a³ N_{A}) with 1 pm = 10^{-10} cm. In hcp/ccp with N atoms: octahedral voids = N, tetrahedral voids = 2N, total voids = 3N. In x g of metal: particles = xn/(ρa³), unit cells = x/(ρa³); in volume V: unit cells = V/a³.

Recent HSC papers consistently test: (1) a 1-mark MCQ on CN, n, r–a relation or defect examples; (2) a 2-mark numerical on ρ = nM/(a³ N_{A}) or predicting lattice type n; (3) a 2-mark theory question on Schottky, impurity, metal deficiency or F-centre defects.

checks.q: Aluminium crystallises in a cubic close-packed (fcc) structure with unit cell edge length 353.6 pm. Calculate the radius of an Al atom.
checks.hint: For ccp/fcc, r = a / (2√2) = 0.3535a.

checks.q: A compound forms an hcp structure. What are the numbers of octahedral voids and tetrahedral voids respectively in 0.5 mol of the substance?
checks.hint: First find N = 0.5 × N_{A}; octahedral voids = N and tetrahedral voids = 2N.

checks.q: Cesium chloride crystallises in a cubic unit cell with Cl^{-} ions at the 8 corners and one Cs^{+} ion at the body centre. How many CsCl formula units are present in one unit cell?
checks.hint: Count Cl^{-} ions (8 corners × 1/8) and Cs^{+} ions (1 at body centre) separately.
checks.explain: Cl^{-} ions = 8 × (1/8) = 1; Cs^{+} ion = 1 (entirely inside the cube). Thus there is 1 CsCl formula unit per unit cell (Exercise 3(viii)).

board.text: An element with molar mass 27 g/mol forms a cubic unit cell with edge length 405 pm. If density of the crystal is 2.7 g cm^{-3}, identify the type of unit cell.
board.answer: Given: M = 27 g mol^{-1}, a = 405 pm = 4.05 × 10^{-8} cm, ρ = 2.7 g cm^{-3}, N_{A} = 6.022 × 10^{23} mol^{-1}. Using ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}), n = ρ a³ N_{A} / M = [2.7 × (4.05 × 10^{-8})³ × 6.022 × 10^{23}] / 27 = 0.1 × 6.643 × 6.022 = 4.00 ≈ 4. Since there are 4 particles per unit cell, the unit cell is face-centred cubic (fcc or ccp).

points.text: Formula n = ρ a³ N_{A} / M, conversion a = 4.05 × 10^{-8} cm and correct substitution
Calculation n ≈ 4 and identification: face-centred cubic (fcc / ccp) unit cell

board.text: Define a unit cell. Which colour is shown by NaCl crystal due to formation of F-centre?
board.answer: Unit cell: The smallest repeating structural unit of a crystalline solid is called a unit cell. Colour of NaCl: NaCl crystal shows yellow colour due to the formation of F-centres (anion vacancies occupied by trapped electrons).

points.text: Definition: the smallest repeating structural unit of a crystalline solid
Colour shown by NaCl crystal due to F-centre: yellow colour

board.text: Schottky defect is NOT observed in _____.
board.answer: (d) NiO. NaCl, KCl and AgBr show Schottky defect, whereas NiO exhibits non-stoichiometric metal deficiency defect (Ni_{0.97}O_{1.0}).

points.text: Correct option (d) NiO

board.text: Derive the relationship between molar mass, density of the substance and unit cell edge length.
board.answer: Let the edge length of a cubic unit cell be a, so its volume is a³. If the mass of one particle is m and there are n particles per unit cell, mass of the unit cell = m × n, and density ρ = (mass of unit cell) / (volume of unit cell) = (m × n) / a³. Molar mass M = m × N_{A}, so m = M / N_{A}. Substituting m gives ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}).

points.text: Volume of unit cell = a³, mass = m × n, and density ρ = (m × n) / a³
Substitute m = M / N_{A} to obtain ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A})

board.text: Predict the type of cubic lattice of a solid element having edge length of 400 pm and density is 6.25 g/ml. (Atomic mass of element = 60)

points.text: Formula n = ρ a³ N_{A} / M, conversion a = 4.00 × 10^{-8} cm and correct substitution
Calculation n ≈ 4 and prediction: face-centred cubic (fcc) lattice

board.text: The number of particles present in Face Centred Cubic Unit Cell is/are _____.
board.answer: (d) 4. An fcc unit cell has 8 corner particles (8 × 1/8 = 1) plus 6 face-centre particles (6 × 1/2 = 3), giving 4 particles in total.

points.text: Correct option (d) 4

board.text: Explain the following terms: (a) Substitutional impurity defect (b) Interstitial impurity defect.
board.answer: (a) Substitutional impurity defect: Foreign atoms occupy regular lattice sites in place of host atoms, displacing regular host atoms. Example: In brass (Cu–Zn alloy), Zn impurity atoms replace host Cu atoms at regular lattice sites (or Sr^{2+} replacing Na^{+} in NaCl). (b) Interstitial impurity defect: Impurity atoms occupy the interstitial spaces (voids) of the host crystal lattice. Example: In steel, Fe atoms occupy normal lattice sites while carbon atoms occupy interstitial spaces.

points.text: (a) Substitutional impurity defect: foreign atoms replace host atoms at regular lattice sites, with example (e.g. Zn in brass or SrCl_{2} in NaCl)
(b) Interstitial impurity defect: foreign atoms occupy interstitial spaces in the lattice, with example (e.g. C atoms in Fe lattice of steel)

board.text: Silver crystallizes in fcc structure. If edge length of unit cell is 400 pm, calculate density of silver (Atomic mass of Ag = 108).

points.text: Formula ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) with n = 4, a = 4.00 × 10^{-8} cm and correct substitution
Final answer 11.21 g cm^{-3} with correct unit

board.text: The relation between radius of sphere and edge length in body centered cubic lattice is given by formula:
board.answer: (c) r = (√3 / 4) a. In a bcc unit cell, spheres touch along the body diagonal of length √3 a, so 4r = √3 a and r = (√3 / 4) a.

points.text: Correct option (c) r = (√3 / 4) a

board.text: Write the consequences of Schottky defect with reasons.
board.answer: 1. Decrease in density: Because ions are missing from their lattice sites, the mass of the solid decreases while its volume remains unchanged; hence density decreases. 2. Preservation of electrical neutrality: Because equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from the lattice, the overall electrical neutrality of the ionic compound is preserved.

points.text: Density decreases because mass decreases due to missing ions while volume remains unchanged
Electrical neutrality is preserved because equal numbers of cations and anions are missing

board.text: Gold crystallises into face-centred cubic cells. The edge length of unit cell is 4.08 × 10^{-8} cm. Calculate the density of gold. [Molar mass of gold = 197 g mol^{-1}]

points.text: Formula ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}) with n = 4 and correct substitution
Final answer 19.27 g cm^{-3} with correct unit

board.text: Explain metal deficiency defect with example.
board.answer: Metal deficiency defect is a non-stoichiometric defect possible only in compounds of metals showing variable oxidation states. Some positive metal ions are missing from their regular lattice sites, and the resulting deficiency of positive charge is balanced by the presence of cations of the same metal in a higher oxidation state at other lattice sites. Example: In NiO, one Ni^{2+} ion is missing from its lattice site and the two missing positive charges are compensated by two Ni^{3+} ions at other Ni^{2+} sites, giving the composition Ni_{0.97}O_{1.0}.

points.text: Explanation: occurs in metals with variable oxidation states; missing cations are charge-balanced by cations of the same metal in a higher oxidation state
Example: in NiO, one missing Ni^{2+} is balanced by two Ni^{3+} ions, yielding Ni_{0.97}O_{1.0}

board.text: The co-ordination number of atoms in body centred cubic structure (bcc) is _____.
board.answer: (c) 8. In a bcc lattice, each atom touches 8 nearest neighbours—four in the layer above and four in the layer below.

points.text: Correct option (c) 8

board.text: Distinguish between crystalline solids and amorphous solids (any four points).
board.answer: 1. Particle arrangement: Crystalline solids have a regular, periodic long-range order; amorphous solids have random arrangement with only short-range order. 2. Melting point: Crystalline solids melt at a sharp, definite temperature; amorphous solids soften and melt gradually over a temperature range. 3. Isotropy: Crystalline solids (except cubic) are anisotropic; amorphous solids are isotropic. 4. Nature & examples: Crystalline solids are true solids (NaCl, diamond, Cu); amorphous solids are supercooled liquids (glass, plastic, rubber).

points.text: Arrangement & melting point: long-range order with sharp m.p. (crystalline) vs short-range order with melting range (amorphous)
Isotropy & nature/examples: anisotropic true solids like NaCl/diamond vs isotropic supercooled liquids like glass/rubber

board.text: Distinguish between ionic solids and molecular solids.
board.answer: 1. Constituent particles: Ionic solids consist of cations and anions; molecular solids consist of monoatomic or polyatomic molecules. 2. Interparticle forces: Ionic solids are held by strong electrostatic forces; molecular solids are held by weak London, dipole-dipole or hydrogen-bond forces. 3. Hardness & melting point: Ionic solids are hard, brittle and high-melting (600 °C–3000 °C); molecular solids are soft and low-melting (−272 °C to 400 °C). 4. Electrical conductivity: Ionic solids conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution (e.g. NaCl, CaF_{2}); molecular solids are poor conductors/insulators (e.g. ice, benzoic acid).

points.text: Particles & forces: cations/anions with strong electrostatic forces (ionic) vs molecules with weak London, dipole-dipole or H-bonds (molecular)
Properties & examples: hard, brittle, high m.p., conduct when molten/aqueous (NaCl) vs soft, low m.p., insulators (ice, CO_{2})

board.text: Distinguish between metallic conductors, insulators and semiconductors on the basis of band theory.
board.answer: 1. Metallic conductors: Have a partially filled conduction band (e.g. 3s band in Na) or overlapping filled valence and empty conduction bands (e.g. 3s and 3p in Mg) with zero band gap; electrons move freely, giving high conductivity (10^{4}–10^{7} Ω^{-1}m^{-1}) that decreases on heating. 2. Insulators: Have a completely filled valence band and an empty conduction band separated by a large band gap (forbidden zone, e.g. diamond 5.47 eV); thermal energy cannot promote electrons, so conductivity is very low (10^{-20}–10^{-10} Ω^{-1}m^{-1}). 3. Semiconductors: Have a filled valence band and empty conduction band separated by a small band gap (Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.67 eV); electrons thermally jump to the conduction band, giving intermediate conductivity (10^{-6}–10^{4} Ω^{-1}m^{-1}) that increases with temperature.

points.text: Metallic conductors: partially filled conduction band or overlapping bands, zero band gap, high conductivity (10^{4}–10^{7} Ω^{-1}m^{-1})
Insulators: filled valence band and empty conduction band separated by a large forbidden zone, very low conductivity (10^{-20}–10^{-10} Ω^{-1}m^{-1})
Semiconductors: small band gap (Si, Ge), electrons thermally promoted to conduction band, conductivity increases with temperature (10^{-6}–10^{4} Ω^{-1}m^{-1})

board.text: What are n-type and p-type semiconductors? Explain how doping pure silicon with phosphorus and with boron increases its conductivity.
board.answer: n-type semiconductor: Formed by doping a group-14 semiconductor (Si or Ge) with a group-15 element (P, As, Sb, Bi). Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons: 4 form covalent bonds with neighbouring Si atoms, and the 5th extra electron enters the conduction band and moves freely under an applied potential, raising conductivity. p-type semiconductor: Formed by doping Si or Ge with a group-13 element (B, Ga, In). Boron has only 3 valence electrons, forming 3 bonds with Si and leaving an electron vacancy (hole) in the valence band. Electrons move into adjacent holes under an applied field so holes act as mobile positive charge carriers, increasing conductivity while the crystal stays electrically neutral.

points.text: n-type: Si doped with group-15 element (P); 4 valence electrons bond and the 5th extra electron enters the conduction band as a mobile negative carrier
p-type: Si doped with group-13 element (B); 3 valence electrons bond, creating an electron vacancy (hole) in the valence band acting as a positive carrier
Conductivity rises due to extra conduction-band electrons (n-type) or valence-band holes (p-type), while overall electrical neutrality is maintained

derivations.title: Packing efficiency of simple cubic (sc) lattice (52.36%)
derivations.given: A metal crystallises in a simple cubic unit cell of edge length a. Corner spheres of radius r touch each other along the cube edge.

steps.line: Corner spheres touch along the edge, so a = 2r and hence r = a/2
wrong: a = 4r and hence r = a/4
√2 a = 4r and hence r = a/(2√2)
steps.note: See Fig 1.9: two corner radii span one cube edge.

steps.line: Volume of one spherical particle: V_{1} = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(a/2)³ = πa³/6
A simple cubic unit cell contains n = 1 particle (8 × 1/8 = 1), so occupied volume = πa³/6
wrong: A simple cubic unit cell contains n = 2 particles, so occupied volume = πa³/3
A simple cubic unit cell contains n = 8 particles, so occupied volume = 4πa³/3

steps.line: Packing efficiency = (volume occupied / volume of unit cell) × 100 = [(πa³/6) / a³] × 100 = 100π / 6
wrong: Packing efficiency = [a³ / (πa³/6)] × 100 = 600 / π
Packing efficiency = (π / 8) × 100

steps.line: Substituting π = 3.142 gives (100 × 3.142) / 6 = 52.36% (void volume = 47.64%)
wrong: Substituting π = 3.142 gives 68% (void volume = 32%)
Substituting π = 3.142 gives 74% (void volume = 26%)

derivations.title: Packing efficiency of body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice (68%)
derivations.given: A metal crystallises in a bcc unit cell of edge length a. The body-centre sphere touches two corner spheres along the cube body diagonal AF (Fig 1.10).

steps.line: By Pythagoras theorem: face diagonal FD² = a² + a² = 2a², and body diagonal AF² = a² + FD² = 3a², so AF = √3 a
wrong: Body diagonal AF² = a² + a² = 2a², so AF = √2 a
Body diagonal AF = 3a

steps.line: Along the body diagonal, spheres touch so AF = 4r; hence √3 a = 4r and r = (√3 / 4) a
wrong: AF = 2r; hence √3 a = 2r and r = (√3 / 2) a
√2 a = 4r and hence r = (√2 / 4) a
steps.note: This exact relation was asked in 2023 Q1(i).

steps.line: Volume of one sphere: (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π[(√3 / 4)a]³ = (4/3)π(3√3 / 64)a³ = (√3 π a³) / 16
wrong: Volume of one sphere = (3 π a³) / 16
Volume of one sphere = (√3 π a³) / 8

steps.line: A bcc unit cell contains n = 2 particles (8 × 1/8 + 1), so total occupied volume = 2 × (√3 π a³ / 16) = (√3 π a³) / 8
wrong: A bcc unit cell contains n = 4 particles, so total occupied volume = (√3 π a³) / 4
A bcc unit cell contains n = 1 particle, so total occupied volume = (√3 π a³) / 16

steps.line: Packing efficiency = [(√3 π a³ / 8) / a³] × 100 = (√3 π / 8) × 100 = 68% (void volume = 32%)
wrong: Packing efficiency = (√3 π / 16) × 100 = 34% (void volume = 66%)
Packing efficiency = (π / 6) × 100 = 52.36% (void volume = 47.64%)

derivations.title: Packing efficiency of face-centred cubic (fcc) lattice (74%)
derivations.given: A metal crystallises in an fcc (ccp) unit cell of edge length a. Corner spheres touch the face-centre sphere along the face diagonal AC (Fig 1.11).

steps.line: In right-angled triangle ABC on a face, face diagonal AC² = a² + a² = 2a², so AC = √2 a
wrong: Face diagonal AC² = a² + 2a² = 3a², so AC = √3 a
Face diagonal AC = 2a

steps.line: Along the face diagonal AC = 4r; hence √2 a = 4r, giving r = (√2 / 4)a = a / (2√2)
wrong: Along the face diagonal AC = 2r, giving r = (√2 / 2)a
Along the face diagonal √3 a = 4r, giving r = (√3 / 4)a

steps.line: Volume of one sphere: (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π[a / (2√2)]³ = (4/3)πa³ / (16√2) = πa³ / (12√2)
wrong: Volume of one sphere = πa³ / (6√2)
Volume of one sphere = πa³ / (3√2)

steps.line: An fcc unit cell contains n = 4 particles (8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2), so total occupied volume = 4 × πa³ / (12√2) = πa³ / (3√2)
wrong: An fcc unit cell contains n = 2 particles, so total occupied volume = πa³ / (6√2)
An fcc unit cell contains n = 6 particles, so total occupied volume = πa³ / (2√2)

steps.line: Packing efficiency = [(πa³ / (3√2)) / a³] × 100 = [π / (3√2)] × 100 = 74% (void volume = 26%)
wrong: Packing efficiency = [π / (12√2)] × 100 = 18.5% (void volume = 81.5%)
Packing efficiency = (√3 π / 8) × 100 = 68% (void volume = 32%)

derivations.title: Density, molar mass and edge length relation, ρ = nM/(a³ N_{A})
derivations.given: A crystalline substance has a cubic unit cell of edge length a containing n particles, each of mass m. Its molar mass is M and Avogadro's number is N_{A}.

steps.line: Volume of the cubic unit cell of edge length a is V = a³
wrong: Volume of the cubic unit cell is V = 6a²
Volume of the cubic unit cell is V = (4/3)πa³

steps.line: With n particles of mass m each, mass of the unit cell = m × n
wrong: Mass of the unit cell = m / n
Mass of the unit cell = M × n

steps.line: Density of the substance equals density of the unit cell: ρ = (mass of unit cell) / (volume of unit cell) = (m × n) / a³
wrong: ρ = a³ / (m × n)
ρ = (m × n) × a³

steps.line: Molar mass is the mass of N_{A} particles: M = m × N_{A}, therefore m = M / N_{A}
wrong: M = m / N_{A}, therefore m = M × N_{A}
m = N_{A} / M

steps.line: Substituting m = M / N_{A} into the density equation yields ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A})
wrong: Substituting gives ρ = (n M N_{A}) / a³
Substituting gives ρ = (M a³) / (n N_{A})

derivations.title: Number of particles and unit cells in x g of metal
derivations.given: A metallic crystal of density ρ and molar mass M has cubic unit cells of edge length a with n particles per unit cell. Find the number of particles and unit cells in x g of the metal.

steps.line: From ρ = nM / (a³ N_{A}), express molar mass as M = ρ a³ N_{A} / n
wrong: Express molar mass as M = (n ρ) / (a³ N_{A})
Express molar mass as M = (a³ N_{A}) / (ρ n)

steps.line: Since molar mass M contains N_{A} particles, x g of metal contains (x N_{A}) / M particles
wrong: x g of metal contains (x M) / N_{A} particles
x g of metal contains M / (x N_{A}) particles

steps.line: Substitute M = ρ a³ N_{A} / n: number of particles in x g = (x N_{A}) / (ρ a³ N_{A} / n) = xn / (ρa³)
wrong: Number of particles in x g = x / (n ρ a³)
Number of particles in x g = (x ρ a³) / n

steps.line: Because n particles correspond to 1 unit cell, number of unit cells in x g = [xn / (ρa³)] × (1 / n)
wrong: Number of unit cells in x g = [xn / (ρa³)] × n
Number of unit cells in x g = [xn / (ρa³)] / N_{A}

steps.line: Cancelling n gives: number of unit cells in x g of metal = x / (ρa³) (and in volume V of metal = V / a³)
wrong: Number of unit cells in x g of metal = (ρa³) / x
Number of unit cells in x g of metal = xn / (ρa³)
